sequences.title: Only $e^{Dt}$ changes with time
sequences.summary: In $x(t) = Te^{Dt}T^{-1}x(0)$ the eigenvector matrices are constant; the diagonal $e^{Dt}$ holds one exponential per eigenvalue, and $x(t)$ is a blend of those modes. One growing mode takes over almost every start.

initial.title: The solution from the last lecture
initial.explanation: With $[T, D] = \mathrm{eig}(A)$ the solution of $\dot x = Ax$ is $x(t) = Te^{Dt}T^{-1}x(0)$. Stability asks what this does as $t \to \infty$.

steps.title: Only $e^{Dt}$ depends on $t$
steps.explanation: $T$, $T^{-1}$ and $x(0)$ are fixed numbers. Whatever happens as $t \to \infty$ must come from $e^{Dt}$.

steps.title: $e^{Dt}$ is diagonal
steps.explanation: $D$ holds the eigenvalues on its diagonal, so $e^{Dt}$ holds one exponential $e^{\lambda_i t}$ per eigenvalue and zeros elsewhere. Each is a mode with its own rate.

steps.title: $x(t)$ is a blend of modes
steps.tex: x(t) = z_1(0)\,e^{\lambda_1 t}c_1 + \cdots + z_n(0)\,e^{\lambda_n t}c_n,\qquad z(0) = T^{-1}x(0)
steps.explanation: Split $T$ into its eigenvector columns $c_i$ and write $z(0) = T^{-1}x(0)$. Each mode $e^{\lambda_i t}$ is carried along its eigenvector with the fixed weight $z_i(0)$: the lecturer's mixture.

steps.title: One growing mode takes over
steps.explanation: Example rates $\lambda_1 = -1$, $\lambda_2 = 0.6$ and weights $z_1 = 1$, $z_2 = 0.08$ (the plotted curves). The decaying mode fades while the growing one, however small at first, dominates the blend. Any $z_2 \neq 0$ makes $|x(t)|$ grow without bound; a random start has $z_2 \neq 0$.

steps.title: Unless the start avoids that mode
steps.explanation: A start with no component along the unstable eigenvector decays. But stability is a property of all starts, so the system is still unstable. Rounding errors or disturbances may still give this start a small unstable component.

sequences.title: Complex eigenvalues: envelope times rotation
sequences.summary: Euler's formula splits $e^{(a+ib)t}$ into the envelope $e^{at}$ and a factor of size one; the real part decides growth or decay. Conjugate pairs give real solutions.

initial.title: A complex eigenvalue
initial.explanation: Eigenvalues may be complex: real part $a$, imaginary part $b$.

steps.title: Put $\lambda$ in the exponent
steps.explanation: The mode of this eigenvalue is $e^{\lambda t}$. Substitute $\lambda = a + ib$.

steps.title: Split the exponent
steps.explanation: $e^{u + v} = e^u e^v$ also holds for complex numbers: a real exponential times a purely imaginary one.

steps.title: Euler's formula
steps.explanation: $e^{ibt}$ is the point at angle $bt$ on the unit circle. As $t$ grows it just goes round and round.

steps.title: The size is $e^{at}$
steps.tex: |e^{\lambda t}| = e^{at}\,|\cos bt + i\sin bt| = e^{at}
steps.explanation: $|\cos bt + i\sin bt| = 1$ for every $t$, so only the real part $a$ sets the amplitude.

steps.title: $a > 0$: growing envelope
steps.explanation: The real part of the mode oscillates at frequency $b$ inside the envelope $\pm e^{at}$. With $a > 0$ the envelope grows exponentially: the oscillation blows up.

steps.title: $a < 0$: decaying envelope
steps.explanation: Slide $a$ through zero to $-0.5$: the same oscillation now sits inside a shrinking envelope and decays to zero. $b$ never changes the verdict.

steps.title: Conjugate pairs: imaginary parts cancel
steps.explanation: A real $A$ has complex eigenvalues in pairs $a \pm ib$. Adding the pair, the $\pm i\sin bt$ terms cancel and a real oscillation in the envelope remains.

sequences.title: The stable left half-plane
sequences.summary: Draw the eigenvalues in the complex plane: all in the open left half-plane means every solution decays; one in the right half-plane means unstable. Control later moves eigenvalues left.

initial.title: Where are the eigenvalues?
initial.explanation: Each eigenvalue is a point in the complex plane: real part across, imaginary part up.

steps.title: Eigenvalues as points
steps.explanation: An example with one real eigenvalue and a conjugate pair, mirror images across the real axis.

steps.title: Left half-plane: every mode decays
steps.explanation: All three eigenvalues have negative real part, so every $e^{\lambda_i t}$ shrinks and every solution decays to $0$. The lecturer states this as stable if and only if all real parts are negative.

steps.title: Cross the axis: unstable
steps.explanation: Move the pair to $0.4 \pm 1.5i$. One eigenvalue (here a pair) in the right half-plane is enough: its growing envelope blows up.

steps.title: Preview: control moves eigenvalues
steps.tex: \dot x = Ax + Bu:\ \text{choose } u \text{ to drag eigenvalues left (later lectures)}
steps.explanation: As the lecturer sketches at 7:59, the goal of feedback control will be to push unstable eigenvalues back into the left half-plane. How is taught in later lectures.

steps.title: The inverted pendulum
steps.explanation: The upright pendulum has a positive real eigenvalue, so it falls. The book's example (p. 335) gives $\lambda = \pm\sqrt{g/L}$; here drawn with $g/L = 2.25$.

sequences.title: Supplement: eigenvalues on the boundary
sequences.summary: Not covered in the lecture. With the largest real part exactly $0$, semisimple eigenvalues give bounded solutions that never decay (Lyapunov stability), while a Jordan block grows like $t$. The discrete-time twin lives on the unit circle.

initial.title: Supplement: what if the largest real part is 0?
initial.explanation: The lecture's criterion covers strictly negative and positive real parts. This supplement looks at the case in between.

steps.title: Pendulum down: onto the imaginary axis
steps.explanation: Flipping the pendulum to hang down rotates its eigenvalues from $\pm\sqrt{g/L}$ to $\pm i\sqrt{g/L}$ (book p. 335): exactly on the imaginary axis.

steps.title: Semisimple: bounded, never decaying
steps.explanation: For $J = \begin{bmatrix}0&-\omega\\ \omega&0\end{bmatrix}$ ($\lambda = \pm i\omega$) the exponential is a rotation: solutions circle forever. Bounded but not decaying: Lyapunov stable, not asymptotically stable.

steps.title: Defective: a Jordan block grows
steps.explanation: A repeated eigenvalue $0$ with only one eigenvector: $J^2 = 0$, so the series stops after $I + Jt$. Then $x_1(t) = x_1(0) + t\,x_2(0)$ grows linearly: unstable, with no positive real part anywhere.

steps.title: Discrete twin and summary
steps.explanation: On the unit circle the same split happens: semisimple eigenvalues keep $|\tilde\lambda^N| = 1$, a Jordan block grows like $N$. Summary: asymptotic needs all strictly inside; boundary is Lyapunov only if semisimple.

sequences.title: Sampling: $x_{k+1} = \tilde A x_k$
sequences.summary: Measuring every $\Delta t$ turns the flow into a one-step map: $x_{k+1} = e^{A\Delta t}x_k$, so $x_N = \tilde A^N x_0$.

initial.title: A continuous solution
initial.explanation: The state varies continuously in time. An experiment or a digital controller does not see all of it.

steps.title: Measure every $\Delta t$
steps.explanation: Keep only the values at the sample times $0, \Delta t, 2\Delta t, \dots$ and number them $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$

steps.title: One step is a matrix exponential
steps.tex: x_{k+1} = e^{A(k+1)\Delta t}x(0) = e^{A\Delta t}\,e^{Ak\Delta t}x(0) = e^{A\Delta t}\,x_k
steps.explanation: Split the exponential with $e^{A(s+t)} = e^{As}e^{At}$; the right-hand factor applied to $x(0)$ is exactly $x_k$. No approximation is involved.

steps.title: Name the step matrix $\tilde A$
steps.explanation: The lecture calls it $\tilde A$; the book writes $A_d$ (Eq. 8.22a). Each hop from one sample to the next is multiplication by $\tilde A$.

steps.title: Iterate
steps.tex: x_1 = \tilde A x_0,\quad x_2 = \tilde A x_1 = \tilde A^2 x_0,\quad x_3 = \tilde A^3 x_0
steps.explanation: Substitute $x_1 = \tilde Ax_0$ into $x_2 = \tilde Ax_1$ to get $\tilde A^2x_0$, and so on.

steps.title: Powers replace the exponential
steps.explanation: In discrete time the question of stability becomes: what happens to $\tilde A^N$ as $N \to \infty$?

sequences.title: Powers of $\tilde\lambda$ and the unit circle
sequences.summary: $\tilde A^N = \tilde T\tilde D^N\tilde T^{-1}$, and $\tilde\lambda^N = r^Ne^{iN\theta}$: the radius decides. Stable if and only if every eigenvalue is inside the unit circle.

initial.title: Powers of the step matrix
initial.tex: x_N = \tilde A^N x_0,\qquad \tilde A\tilde T = \tilde T\tilde D
initial.explanation: Diagonalize $\tilde A$ exactly like $A$: its eigenvectors go in the columns of $\tilde T$, its eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\tilde D$.

steps.title: Solve for $\tilde A$
steps.tex: \tilde A\tilde T = \tilde T\tilde D \;\Rightarrow\; \tilde A = \tilde T\tilde D\tilde T^{-1}
steps.explanation: Multiply on the right by $\tilde T^{-1}$; $\tilde T\tilde T^{-1} = I$ on the left. This is the board derivation at 16:44 (aloud at 12:57 the lecturer says $T^{-1}DT$, unsure of the order).

steps.title: Inner pairs cancel
steps.tex: \tilde A^3 = \tilde T\tilde D\cancel{\tilde T^{-1}\tilde T}\tilde D\cancel{\tilde T^{-1}\tilde T}\tilde D\tilde T^{-1} = \tilde T\tilde D^3\tilde T^{-1},\qquad \tilde A^N = \tilde T\tilde D^N\tilde T^{-1}
steps.explanation: Writing $\tilde A$ three times, each adjacent $\tilde T^{-1}\tilde T$ is $I$. Only the diagonal matrix gets powered: $\tilde D^N = \mathrm{diag}(\tilde\lambda_i^N)$.

steps.title: Radius and angle
steps.explanation: Any complex number is a radius $r$ and an angle $\theta$; real part $r\cos\theta$, imaginary part $r\sin\theta$.

steps.title: Powers turn and scale
steps.explanation: Each multiplication adds $\theta$ to the angle and multiplies the radius by $r$. With $r = 0.88$ the powers spiral in; with $r = 1.1$ they spiral out.

steps.title: Inside the unit circle
steps.explanation: Stable if and only if every eigenvalue of $\tilde A$ is strictly inside the unit circle; one outside makes the system unstable.

steps.title: Magnitude, not real part
steps.explanation: At 16:10 the lecturer says real part, but the radius is what counts. This eigenvalue has a small real part and still lies outside the circle: unstable.

sequences.title: $e^{\lambda\Delta t}$: left half-plane to unit disc
sequences.summary: The eigenvalues of $e^{A\Delta t}$ are $e^{\lambda\Delta t}$. Vertical lines become circles, the imaginary axis the unit circle, horizontal lines rays: the two stability criteria agree.

initial.title: Two complex planes
initial.explanation: Left: eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $A$. Right: eigenvalues $\tilde\lambda$ of the sampled $\tilde A$, with the unit circle.

steps.title: Same eigenvectors, eigenvalues $e^{\lambda\Delta t}$
steps.tex: e^{A\Delta t} = T\,e^{D\Delta t}\,T^{-1} \;\Rightarrow\; \tilde\lambda_i = e^{\lambda_i\Delta t}
steps.explanation: From $A = TDT^{-1}$, the exponential keeps the eigenvectors and exponentiates each eigenvalue.

steps.title: Radius from Re, angle from Im
steps.tex: e^{(a+ib)\Delta t} = e^{a\Delta t}\,e^{ib\Delta t}:\quad |\tilde\lambda| = e^{a\Delta t},\ \arg\tilde\lambda = b\Delta t
steps.explanation: Here $\Delta t = 1$: $\lambda = -0.5 + 1.2i$ lands at radius $e^{-0.5} \approx 0.61$ and angle $1.2$ rad.

steps.title: Vertical lines become circles
steps.explanation: Every point of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = -0.5$ has the same radius after the map, so the line wraps onto a circle of radius $e^{-0.5}$.

steps.title: Imaginary axis to unit circle, half-plane to disc
steps.explanation: Lines further left give smaller circles; the imaginary axis gives the unit circle. The left half-plane fills the inside of the disc, every point except the centre: $e^{\lambda\Delta t}$ is never $0$.

steps.title: Horizontal lines become rays
steps.explanation: Horizontal lines map to rays from the origin (the angle $b\Delta t$ is taken modulo $2\pi$). Circles and rays still meet at right angles, as the grid did: the map is conformal.

steps.title: The upshot
steps.explanation: Continuous time: negative real parts. Discrete time: inside the unit circle. They are the same condition: asymptotic stability depends only on the eigenvalues (exactly on the boundary, the Jordan structure matters too).
